svg.aria-label: 2000–2009 · the executable, from worms to botnets: the five tracks for these years, key events labelled, every dot with its date on hover; the tracks light up one at a time
svg.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: 2000–2009 · the executable, from worms to botnets: the five tracks for these years, key events labelled, every dot with its date on hover; the tracks light up one at a time

circle.title: 2000 · Notoriety — Early-2000s worm authors seek fame rather than money.
2000 · VBScript worms (first script wave) — ILOVEYOU, May 2000; Anna Kournikova, February 2001. Macro viruses had led the way since 1995.

2000 · Outlook blocks executable attachments — Outlook E-mail Security Update, June 2000; mail gateways follow. Office 2000 macro security levels end the first script wave. Attackers answer by diversifying file types.
2000 · Signature antivirus — File scanners and signature databases.
2000 · Plaintext HTTP — HTTPS only for login and payment.
2000 · Mass-mailing worms — Executable attachments and self-mailing worms.
2001 · IE6 and ActiveX — Internet Explorer 6 dominance.
2001 · Code Red, Nimda — Code Red, July 2001 (IIS, MS01-033); Nimda, 18 September 2001: worms that spread over the network with no email and no user action.
2001 · Windows XP — Released 25 October 2001: users run as administrator, autorun on, firewall off by default.
2002 · Packers and protectors — UPX (1998), ASPack, Armadillo; Themida 1.0 in December 2004.
2003 · Heuristics and emulation — Scanners run the file a little to see through packers.
2003 · Slammer — 25 January 2003: one UDP packet exploiting SQL Server (MS02-039), spreading worldwide in minutes.
2003 · Adware, pay-per-install — Infected machines monetized through installs and ads.
2003 · Broadband replaces dial-up — Always-on hosts; email as the delivery channel.
2003 · Blaster — 11 August 2003: exploits the RPC DCOM flaw (MS03-026) on Windows 2000 and XP; Windows XP SP2 turns the firewall on the next year.

2003 · IRC botnets: Agobot, rxbot — 2002–2004: Agobot (Gaobot), SDBot and its rxbot derivatives make the compromised machine join an IRC channel and take orders. Infections become inventory, rented for spam, DDoS and installs.
2004 · Hacker Defender — Windows user-mode rootkit; v1.00 released January 2004.

2004 · Mass-mailers switch to zip (MyDoom, Bagle) — MyDoom, 26 January 2004, mails itself in zip archives; Bagle.F, 29 February 2004, in password-protected zips, the password shown as an image by mid-March. The answer to attachment blocking, within weeks.
2004 · HIPS, anti-spam, VirusTotal — Host intrusion prevention; VirusTotal launched 2004.
2004 · Sasser — 30 April 2004: exploits the Windows logon service, LSASS (MS04-011), with no user action; Windows XP SP2 ships with the firewall on that August.
2004 · Gmail blocks executables, zips included — Documented by June 2004: messages with executable attachments, even inside zip archives, bounce to the sender. Gmail adds .js in February 2017.
2004 · DDoS extortion, DDoS for hire — Botnets flood online businesses for ransom and are rented out for attacks; Ancheta indicted for selling botnet access for DDoS and spam, November 2005.
2004 · XP SP2: firewall on, DEP — Service Pack 2, August 2004.

2005 · IM worms: Bropia, Kelvir — Bropia (January 2005) sends itself as a .pif over MSN Messenger; Kelvir (March 2005) sends a link to it. MSN Messenger 7 blocks .pif and filters executable transfers on 7 April 2005; the links were not covered.
2005 · MSN Messenger 7 filters unsafe transfers — 7 April 2005: .pif messages blocked and executable transfers filtered, after Bropia and Kelvir; links were not covered.
2005 · Kernel Patch Protection (x64) — First shipped 2005 on XP x64 and Server 2003 SP1.
2005 · Botnets for hire: spam, DDoS, click fraud — Botnet capacity rented for spam and DDoS; browsers monetized by click fraud. The infected machine is inventory.

g.text: Botnets for hire: spam, DDoS, click fraud

circle.title: 2005 · Network IDS/IPS — Payload signatures on plaintext traffic.
2005 · Sony BMG rootkit — Disclosed by Mark Russinovich, 31 October 2005.
2006 · Flash, Java, Acrobat plug-ins — The browser exploitation surface of the decade.

2006 · Exploit documents, then MPack (2006–08) — A Word zero-day in targeted attacks, May 2006 (MS06-027); MPack, the first exploit kit sold commercially, documented May–June 2007; a PDF exploit in the wild with zero antivirus detections, November 2008 (CVE-2008-2992).
2006 · Rustock — Kernel rootkit and spam bot, first analysed June 2006.
2007 · Storm Worm — First large spam run 19 January 2007 (F-Secure; detection added 15 January); server-side polymorphism at scale.
2007 · Vista: UAC, signed drivers, ASLR — Consumer release 30 January 2007; mandatory 64-bit driver signing.
2007 · Server-side polymorphism — Thousands of unique variants per day; hashes become one-shot.
2007 · Banking trojans, carding — Credentials and cards become the product.
2007 · Zeus — Banking trojan first identified July 2007.
2007 · Mebroot MBR bootkit — First traces November 2007; drive-by waves December 2007 to January 2008.
2008 · Fake antivirus — Rogue AV scams peak 2008–2011.
2008 · Koobface — Detected 31 July 2008 on MySpace and Facebook: a social-network worm whose botnet earned over US$2 million from pay-per-install and click fraud between June 2009 and June 2010.
2008 · McAfee Artemis — Cloud reputation, announced September 2008.
2008 · Conficker — Conficker.A detected 21 November 2008.
2009 · Symantec Quorum / Insight — File prevalence in Norton 2010, announced September 2009.
2009 · Windows 7 ships PowerShell 2.0 — 22 October 2009: an interpreter on every machine.
